source: Sajid, Ball, Parr, Friston (2021) Active inference: demystified and compared
finding: Anchor study. Reward is recast as a prior preference over outcomes. In FrozenLake (OpenAI Gym) active inference matched Bayesian model-based RL in the deterministic version and beat both RL agents in the stochastic version.
numbers: Table 1, 200 trials x 500 episodes. Deterministic: Q-learning (decaying eps) 97.79 [97.41,98.16] and belief-based Q-learning 80.44 [78.96,81.93]; Bayesian RL 99.76 [99.45,100]; Active inference 99.88 [99.64,100]. Stochastic: Q-learning 66.08 and 65.13; Bayesian RL 64.39 [60.33,68.44]; Active inference 98.90 [98.00,99.79].
quote: reward functions can be absorbed into expected free energy
limits: Small discrete grid. The generative model already knows the goal is at position 6 or 8. Authors say FrozenLake is not representative of discrete environments. The plain-text table lost the eps=0.1 Q-learning row, so the row-to-number mapping for the two Q-learning variants is my best reading.
agent_relevance: A belief model that knows the task structure beats trial-and-error learning. Our scaffold plays that role; the LLM need not learn from reward.

source: Sajid, Ball, Parr, Friston (2021) Active inference: demystified and compared
finding: Null model with flat preferences (reward is just another observation with no weight) scores at chance. The goal and the hole are equally informative, so nothing favours the goal.
numbers: Active inference null model 50.03 [49.70,50.35] deterministic; 50.22 stochastic.
limits: Flat preferences were set by hand. Authors compare this to an RL agent with no reward.
agent_relevance: Exploration alone does not give task success. Open mode needs a separate goal or stopping rule.

source: Sajid, Ball, Parr, Friston (2021) Active inference: demystified and compared
finding: Non-stationary FrozenLake: goal and hole swap at episodes 21, 121, 141, 251, 451. Active inference recovered after one episode. Q-learning and Bayesian RL needed about 40 episodes. Bayesian RL got slower on each swap because pseudo-counts piled up.
numbers: All agents fell to 0 at episode 21 except the null agent. RL recovery about 40 episodes; active inference one episode. Q-learning eps=0.1 adapted fairly quickly.
limits: The advantage comes from a generative model that already contains the two contexts. That is a hand-coded structural prior, not learning.
agent_relevance: Give the agent an explicit set of hypotheses and let evidence switch beliefs, instead of re-learning after a change.

source: Sajid, Ball, Parr, Friston (2021) Active inference: demystified and compared
finding: Reward-free setting: with all rewards at zero, Q-learning learns a circular policy and does not explore. Belief-based agents (Bayesian RL and active inference) keep exploring.
numbers: Table 2 row 1, 100 episodes for 100 agents: Q-learning 0.00 score (15.00 moves); Bayesian RL 39.94 (9.17 moves); Active inference 44.00 (8.67 moves).
limits: Bayesian RL explored almost as much as active inference, so the gain is not unique to active inference. Q-learning was evaluated with eps=0 in this table.
agent_relevance: Basis for an open mode: a belief-based loop explores with no reward and a plain value learner does not.

source: Sajid, Ball, Parr, Friston (2021) Active inference: demystified and compared
finding: Pure exploration test: with likelihood learning only and no preferences, the agent's first trajectory covered new states with no revisits, and later trajectories stayed non-overlapping.
numbers: Simulated 15 times. First trajectory: right(1-2), right(2-3), down(3-6), right(6-6).
limits: Qualitative figures only. No statistics and no comparison to a curiosity-bonus RL agent.
agent_relevance: This is the behaviour wanted in open mode: go where the model is most uncertain and stop revisiting known states.

source: Sajid, Ball, Parr, Friston (2021) Active inference: demystified and compared
finding: Learned preferences can drift to a bad attractor. If the agent keeps falling into the hole, it comes to prefer the hole and goes straight there after about 5 trials.
numbers: Preference learning simulated 10 times per outcome type. Dirichlet priors start at 5 (likelihood) and 1 (preferences).
limits: The authors present this as self-evidencing, a feature. For engineering it is a failure mode.
agent_relevance: A self-updating preference store can lock in what the loop keeps producing. Keep preferences fixed or checked by code.

source: Sajid, Ball, Parr, Friston (2021) Active inference: demystified and compared
finding: Reward-shaping equivalence: when preferences are set to match a reward function, Bayesian RL and active inference behave almost the same. Q-learning is more sensitive to living costs and takes fewer steps.
numbers: Table 2, goal 100, hole 0, living cost -10: Q-learning 95.56 (3.53 moves); Bayesian RL 99.77 (3.02); Active inference 99.52 (3.03). Goal only: 95.32 (3.58), 99.74 (3.00), 99.50 (3.07). The column order of the middle rows was ambiguous in the text.
limits: Equivalence holds in this environment. The authors warn a maze with a noisy attractor and no reward might differ.
agent_relevance: Calling reward a preference is a re-description, not a new capability. Do not expect gains from the label alone.

source: Tschantz, Millidge, Seth, Buckley (2020) Reinforcement learning through active inference
finding: A deep model-based agent that minimises free energy of the expected future (FEEF) handled sparse, shaped and zero-reward tasks with one objective.
numbers: Mountain Car (sparse): optimal in a single trial, 25 episodes of at most 200 steps. Half Cheetah run and flip: better than SAC after 100 episodes (mean of 5 seeds). Ant Maze with no reward: more of the maze covered than random after 35 episodes (mean of 4 seeds).
quote: minimising the free energy of the expected future proves beneficial in environments with no reward
limits: Workshop paper. Returns and coverage values are in figures only. The reward-free baseline was random actions, which is weak. 4 to 5 seeds.
agent_relevance: The information-gain term over model parameters drives sparse-task success. The rule is simple: pick the probe that most reduces uncertainty.

source: Tschantz, Millidge, Seth, Buckley (2020) Reinforcement learning through active inference
finding: Boundary condition: on Cup Catch the exploration term gave little benefit, because random actions already reach the goal.
numbers: Cup Catch results comparable to reward-only and variance baselines.
limits: This is the authors' hypothesis, not tested separately.
agent_relevance: Directed exploration pays only where plain sampling stalls. Add it only for problems where random probing fails.

source: Tschantz, Baltieri, Seth, Buckley (2020) Scaling active inference
finding: Deep active inference with an ensemble transition model explored the continuous MountainCar state space more than a reward-only agent and more than an epsilon-greedy agent (Gaussian action noise, variance 0.3).
numbers: 100 epochs; 5 seed episodes under random actions; 100 batches of 50 per iteration. Coverage given in a figure only.
limits: No numeric coverage in the text. Exploration and exploitation were tested separately, which the authors say.
agent_relevance: Directed exploration beats noise injection in a sparse task.

source: Tschantz, Baltieri, Seth, Buckley (2020) Scaling active inference
finding: On well-shaped control tasks (inverted pendulum, hopper), using only the extrinsic term, the agent learned in under 100 epochs, about an order of magnitude more sample-efficient than model-free DDPG.
numbers: Mean of 5 seeds with 95% interquartile range. DDPG shown over 1500 epochs; the active agent was stopped at 100.
limits: The gain comes mainly from being model-based. The epistemic term was switched off in this test.
agent_relevance: Do not credit active inference for efficiency that any model-based planner gets.

source: Millidge, Tschantz, Seth, Buckley (2020) On the relationship of active inference and control as inference
finding: Formal comparison with control as inference (the probabilistic form behind soft RL). The main difference is how value enters: as a likelihood (CAI) or a prior (AIF). AIF has an expected information gain that CAI lacks, so it explores toward goals. CAI gets only entropy-maximising random exploration.
numbers: Theory only. No experiments.
quote: AIF is endowed with an expected information gain that CAI lacks
limits: The paper lists small other differences (rewards on state-action pairs vs observations). No empirical test of the behaviour gap.
agent_relevance: Gives the clean reason that reward-as-observation changes exploration. Design rule: drive exploration by expected information gain, not noise.

source: Da Costa, Sajid, Parr, Friston, Smith (2022) Reward maximisation through discrete active inference
finding: Proof. Standard active inference gives Bellman-optimal actions only at planning horizon 1. Sophisticated inference (recursive) gives Bellman-optimal actions on any finite horizon, in MDPs with known transitions at the zero-temperature limit.
numbers: Theorems 15 and 16; horizon-1 result stated in the abstract for POMDPs.
limits: I read the abstract and theorem statements, not the proofs. Known transition probabilities are assumed.
agent_relevance: Active inference need not lose to RL on reward in theory, but only with recursive lookahead. That fits a program-run lookahead, not a single-pass guess.

source: Fountas, Sajid, Mediano, Friston (2020) Deep active inference agents using Monte-Carlo methods
finding: Deep active inference with tree search and a habitual network. Three expected-free-energy variants collected reward like a reward-maximising baseline in dynamic dSprites, but visited more positions and predicted reward better.
numbers: Reward per round similar across agents; positions visited per round higher for active inference; reward reconstruction error lower than baseline (Fig 3). Values in figures only.
limits: Toy task plus Animal-AI. Reward is encoded as a prior preference, so there is no real reward-free test.
agent_relevance: Exploration came at no cost to reward in this toy task. It does not show a win on reward itself.

source: Krishnamurthy, Harris, Foster, Zhang, Slivkins (2024) Can large language models explore in-context?
finding: Language models fail to explore in bandits unless heavily scaffolded. Only one configuration worked: GPT-4, buttons scenario, suggestive framing, externally summarised history, reinforced chain of thought, temperature 0.
numbers: Hard instance: K=5 arms, gap 0.2, T=100. GPT-3.5 over 48 prompt configurations with N=20; baselines 1000 replicates.
quote: all but one of the LLM configurations we consider exhibit exploration failures
limits: The summarised history was built by code, not by the model. Small bandit; authors say external summaries may not scale to complex settings.
agent_relevance: Two failure modes matter for open mode: never retrying the best option, and spreading evenly. The fix is code that keeps counts, which matches our program-decides design.

source: Krishnamurthy, Harris, Foster, Zhang, Slivkins (2024) Can large language models explore in-context?
finding: Longer runs did not repair the base failure. GPT-4 with the basic prompt at T=500 showed suffix failures in over 60% of replicates, like a Greedy algorithm. The working configuration (T=200, N=40) had very few suffix failures.
numbers: Basic prompt: suffix failure in more than 60% of 20 replicates at T=500. Working config: unimodal best-arm pulls over 40 replicates.
limits: Only one working configuration out of many tested, so the result is brittle.
agent_relevance: Counts kept by code are the dependable part. Do not trust the model to track what it has not tried.

source: Binz and Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 on the horizon task (two-armed bandit) showed rough random exploration but no directed exploration, and it ignored the horizon. Humans do both.
numbers: Random exploration beta=0.18+-0.01, z=14.48, p<.001. Interaction with horizon beta=-0.02+-0.02, p=.14. Directed exploration (horizon effect) beta=-0.15+-0.27, p=.58.
limits: Old model (GPT-3) and a text version of the task. Later models are not tested in this paper.
agent_relevance: The model earns decent reward but does not seek information on purpose. Information seeking must come from the scaffold.

source: Binz and Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 beat humans on total regret in the bandit task while showing no directed exploration. Good reward can hide absent information seeking.
numbers: Regret GPT-3 M=2.72 (SD 5.98) vs humans M=3.24 (SD 10.26), t(38878)=-5.03, p<.001. Short horizon: no difference, p=.97.
limits: Reward and exploration signatures are different tests. One model.
agent_relevance: Judge open-mode quality by information gained, not by task reward.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: an open-ended embodied agent with large language models
finding: A GPT-4 agent with an automatic curriculum that maximises exploration, and no reward, beat ReAct, Reflexion and AutoGPT on Minecraft tech-tree speed. A working reward-free exploration loop in an LLM agent.
numbers: Prompting iterations to wooden tool: Voyager 6+-2 (3/3), AutoGPT 92+-72 (3/3), ReAct 0/3, Reflexion 0/3. Iron tool: Voyager 21+-7 vs AutoGPT 135+-103. Diamond: Voyager 1/3 (102 iterations). Headline: 3.3x unique items, 2.3x distance, tech tree up to 15.3x faster.
quote: an automatic curriculum that maximizes exploration
limits: Three runs per method. The LLM picks the curriculum; there is no explicit information-gain computation. Removing self-verification cost 73% of discovered items.
agent_relevance: The closest working example of exploring without reward in an LLM loop. Self-verification, a check, mattered most.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: an open-ended embodied agent with large language models
finding: Plain agent loops stall without exploration pressure. ReAct and Reflexion unlocked no tech-tree level within 160 prompting iterations. AutoGPT reached the iron tool but not diamond.
numbers: ReAct 0/3 and Reflexion 0/3 at every level; AutoGPT 3/3 through iron, 0/3 diamond; Voyager diamond 1/3.
limits: Baselines were adapted by the Voyager authors. Different tool access.
agent_relevance: An exploration mechanism is needed in open mode. A bare reasoning loop does not supply one.

source: CDE (2025) Curiosity-Driven Exploration for efficient reinforcement learning in large language models
finding: A curiosity bonus (actor perplexity, critic value variance) added to reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards gave about +3 points on AIME. Exploration bonuses help even when a reward exists.
numbers: Qwen3-4B-Base GRPO: AIME24 Avg@16 20.8 and AIME25 21.0; with perplexity bonus 23.3 and 23.5. Average over datasets 48.2 to 50.6. PPO baseline average 46.5.
quote: approximate +3 point improvement over standard RLVR
limits: Training-time method that changes weights, so not a prompt scaffold. One model family.
agent_relevance: Background only. It supports the idea that information-seeking terms beat plain reward for language models.

source: Enhancing personalized multi-turn dialogue with curiosity reward (2025)
finding: Intrinsic reward equal to the gain in the model's belief about the user type (an information-gain reward) added to multi-turn RLHF. Authors report better personalisation and generalisation than standard multi-turn RLHF.
numbers: Gemma 2B policy, prompted Gemma 7B as user model; two domains (conversational recommendation, education). Table scores not extracted.
limits: Trained with RL on small models. The user model is itself an LLM. I did not read the result tables closely.
agent_relevance: An LLM-side version of epistemic value: reward questions that sharpen the model of the other party.

source: Active inference for self-organizing multi-LLM systems: a Bayesian thermodynamic approach to adaptation (2024)
finding: An active inference layer (learned Dirichlet observation and transition matrices) chooses prompts and search actions for an LLM research agent by expected free energy. It searched first (about the first 40 steps) and then moved to testing prompts.
numbers: Observation matrices 11x33 for prompts, 11x11 for search, 3x3 for information state. Preferences -32 / 8 / 64 for no / basic / detailed information. GPT-4o-mini scores observations 0.0 to 1.0.
quote: a significant limitation of current LLM-based systems is their reliance on static prompts
limits: No baseline, no accuracy numbers, one run, qualitative figures only.
agent_relevance: Shows the pattern is easy to wire: the LLM is the sensor and code runs the free-energy choice. No evidence yet that it beats a simple bandit.

source: Wen (2025) The missing reward: active inference in the era of experience
finding: Position paper: replace hand-built rewards with free-energy minimisation and use a language model as the generative world model. No experiments. Its energy-saving claims are stated as untested.
numbers: Assumes a 5% cut in retraining energy could save tens of gigawatt-hours. Calls for joules-per-decision benchmarks.
limits: No data. The paper itself calls efficiency validation an open research question.
agent_relevance: Do not cite as evidence. It is a statement of the open-mode idea only.

source: Wen (2025) A framework for inherently safer AGI through language-mediated active inference
finding: Conceptual architecture: beliefs and preferences kept separate in natural language, bounded rationality via free energy, with an ARC research agenda. The paper calls its own work conceptual.
numbers: No experiments. ARC proposed as a future test bed.
limits: No results.
agent_relevance: Its separation of beliefs from preferences mirrors our program-versus-model split. No evidence yet.

source: Know You Before You Speak: user-state modeling for LLM personalization in multi-turn conversation (PUMA) (2026)
finding: PUMA picks dialogue actions by expected free energy over a belief about the user state, using 8B models. It beat counselor baselines on a simulator.
numbers: CAMI, Qwen3-8B: Stage Lift 1.62 vs DIIR 1.07 and CAMI-base 0.62; Prep 75.9% vs 52.0%; TrigCov 62.4% vs 34.0%; turns 12.2 vs 13.1. Llama-3.1-8B: Lift 1.76 vs DIIR 1.17; Prep 83.0%.
limits: Simulated client (DynPatient), gold state labels, greedy decoding, fixed seeds. The ablation table lost its layout in text extraction; removing EFE selection cost roughly 0.17 to 0.28 lift in my reading.
agent_relevance: Best LLM-era test of expected-free-energy action choice. The gain mixes a state tracker with the EFE rule, so EFE alone is not isolated.

source: Know You Before You Speak: user-state modeling for LLM personalization in multi-turn conversation (PUMA) (2026)
finding: Cross-dataset check: PUMA with a small model tracked user state better than a long-prompt baseline with a bigger model.
numbers: CAMI next-state accuracy 0.717 vs long-prompt 0.231. AnnoMI: PUMA Qwen3-8B current 0.639, next 0.532; long-prompt Qwen3-32B 0.602 and 0.430; long-prompt Qwen3-8B 0.463 and 0.364.
limits: Single transfer dataset; label schemes mapped by the authors.
agent_relevance: Structure beat size here. Supports the scaffold bet.
